key_insight: Two automated speech measures, Nasal Cognate Distinctiveness (NCD) and nasal posterior probability (NPP), both tracked hypernasality in motor speech disorders and performed similarly for identifying clinically meaningful nasalization.
clinical_relevance: These tools could support more objective, scalable screening or monitoring of hypernasality in patients with motor speech disorders, potentially beyond stop consonants alone.
method: Analyzed sentence-level speech from 561 participants: 374 neurologically typical controls and 187 with motor speech disorders.
Computed NCD for voiceless stops and NPP for stops, consonants, and vowels using a neural network feature model.
Compared measures against clinician-rated hypernasality using mixed-effects models, correlations, ROC analysis, and test-retest reliability.
evidence_signal: NCD and NPP both changed with hypernasality severity, with comparable discrimination of absent versus present hypernasality and strong inverse correlation across stops; vowel and consonant NPP also showed identical classification performance.
watch_item: Performance was tested on a specific patient cohort and speech task, so broader clinical deployment will need validation across speakers, recording conditions, and disorder types.
paper_title: Automated Assessment of Hypernasality in Motor Speech Disorders Using Nasal Cognate Distinctiveness and Nasal Posterior Probability
